children: Binance plans to begin restoring cryptocurrency withdrawals Sunday following a cyberattack that affected an estimated $6.3 billion in assets, with the exchange saying it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected amount.

For investors, the reopening represents a test of Binance's ability to restore confidence after one of the largest reported cryptocurrency security breaches. The incident has raised concerns about operational security and counterparty risk across the digital asset industry, while the exchange's efforts to replace stolen assets could help limit losses for customers and broader market disruption.

Binance disclosed Friday that the attack affected approximately $6.3 billion in assets, with an initial investigation pointing to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The breach may have allowed attackers to access a service container and initiate unauthorized withdrawals. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been compromised.

The exchange previously reported that approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen on blockchain networks with assistance from industry partners. Binance said Sunday that it had replenished 95% of the impacted assets, up from 90%
. The remaining 5% consists of less liquid tokens that are more difficult to acquire in sufficient quantities.

Binance said balances of major cryptocurrencies and stablecoins, including Bitcoin, Ether, BNB, Solana, XRP, USDT and USDC, are fully backed. The company is using its own resources to replenish affected assets and has pledged to absorb the financial losses rather than pass them on to customers.

The exchange cautioned that withdrawals could experience processing delays during the phased reopening, with additional networks and tokens becoming available as security assessments are completed. Binance also plans to publish a detailed report on the attack once its investigation concludes.
Fully recovered assets include Bitcoin USD

title: Binance to resume crypto withdrawals after $6.3B hack
